extra_misconceptions.fact: Submerged branches act as lethal strainers that let water pass through while pinning boats and paddlers underwater.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Fallen trees overhanging a river bank provide a safe handhold for stopping a canoe in fast current.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Intact blister skin forms a sterile barrier against waterborne bacteria; cover hot spots early with moleskin or medical tape.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Popping a friction blister on the palm with a pocketknife speeds up skin healing on a multi-day canoe trek.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cold water conducts body heat away twenty-five times faster than air at the same temperature, causing rapid core cooling.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Warm air temperatures above seventy degrees eliminate the risk of hypothermia after a canoe capsizes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Low-head dams create a recirculating hydraulic boil at the base that traps boats and swimmers in a drowning cycle.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Calm water just downstream of a low-head dam offers a safe eddy for resting or retrieving a dropped paddle.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a capsized paddler who attempts to stand up in knee-deep moving current above a rocky riverbed?
Which physical indicator distinguishes heat exhaustion from life-threatening heatstroke during an open-water paddle?
Under what weather condition must a canoeing group immediately leave open water and wait thirty minutes on shore?
Why is it dangerous to rewarm a severely hypothermic paddler rapidly with hot packs applied to the arms and legs?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The swimmer test requires seventy-five yards of strong forward strokes followed by twenty-five yards of a resting backstroke.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Completing all one hundred yards using a fast freestyle sprint satisfies the Scouting America swimmer test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Scouting America mandates passing the full swimmer classification test before starting any on-water canoeing requirements.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Paddlers who wear a Coast Guard approved life jacket can skip the swimmer test for flatwater canoeing requirements.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Every candidate must jump feetfirst into water over their head, level off, and begin swimming without pushing off the bottom.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pushing off the pool wall in chest-deep water counts as a valid start for the official swimmer classification test.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The post-swim float requires resting on the back with minimal movement to prove the swimmer can conserve energy in deep water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Vigorous vertical treading with rapid arm and leg motion meets the floating requirement at the end of the swim test.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms the water depth is safe before a Scout jumps feetfirst to begin the swimmer test?
Why must the final twenty-five yards of the swimmer test be completed using an easy, resting backstroke?
Which physical indicator shows that a swimmer is genuinely resting while floating rather than fighting to stay up?
Under what condition must a Scout renew their swimmer classification before participating in a troop canoe trip?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Flat bottoms have high initial stability on calm water but lose secondary stability abruptly when tilted past their bilge edge.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A flat-bottomed canoe hull provides superior stability when leaning into sharp turns or paddling across tall waves.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pronounced rocker lifts the bow and stern so the canoe pivots easily in rapids, whereas a flat keel line tracks straighter.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Heavy hull rocker helps a touring canoe hold a straight course across a windy lake with fewer correction strokes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Thwarts are structural braces that hold the gunwales apart and maintain hull rigidity against water pressure.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Thwarts and the center yoke exist only as handles for lifting or portaging the canoe between lakes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Longer, narrower hulls have a higher hull-speed ceiling and slice through water with far less wave-making drag.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Short, wide canoes glide faster over long distances because they sit higher on top of the water.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a canoe's straight-line tracking when hull rocker increases from flat to banana-shaped?
Which structural hull feature distinguishes initial flatwater steadiness from secondary stability in rough waves?
Where should a builder place tumblehome on a canoe hull to make gunwale-close paddle strokes easier?
What measurement change occurs in hull speed and cargo capacity when a tandem canoe gains two feet of length?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Blade length varies widely by style, so proper paddle sizing depends on the shaft distance between the grip and the throat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Two paddles with the same overall length from grip to tip will fit a paddler identically on the water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Kneeling lowers the paddler's shoulders closer to the waterline, which requires a slightly shorter paddle shaft than sitting.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Kneeling low in the bottom of a canoe requires a longer paddle than sitting high on the bow or stern seat.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Submerging the blade just to the throat maximizes horizontal thrust, whereas burying the shaft wastes energy lifting water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pushing the paddle blade deeper than the throat adds extra leverage and forward speed to each stroke.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The top hand must palm the top of the T-grip or pear grip to steer blade pitch and drive downward cleanly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wrapping all five fingers of the top hand around the paddle shaft below the grip gives better control.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is measuring shaft length from grip to throat more accurate than comparing total paddle height on the ground?
Where should the top of the paddle grip reach when a Scout sizes a paddle while kneeling upright on a dock?
What happens to shoulder strain and blade entry angle when a stern paddler uses a paddle that is six inches too long?
Which blade shape offers the cleanest underwater recovery for quiet, Indian-stroke maneuvering on calm lakes?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cold water shock and waves make donning a floating vest in deep water nearly impossible; always wear it zipped and buckled.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stowing an unzipped life jacket under the canoe seat is safe on calm water because a paddler can put it on after flipping.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coiled rope tangles as it exits the bag; feed the line in loose handfuls from the bottom up so it pays out smoothly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stuffing rescue rope into a throw bag in neat, tied coils prevents knots during an emergency throw.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An oversized vest rides up past the ears in the water and can slip off or push the swimmer's face down.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Buying an oversized adult life jacket for a small Scout is safe as long as every chest buckle is snapped shut.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Safety Afloat requires every participant to wear a properly fitted, Coast Guard approved wearable life jacket at all times.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Any floating seat cushion meets Scouting America life jacket standards for tandem flatwater canoeing.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the shoulder straps during a chin-level tug test if a paddler's life jacket is too loose?
Where should a Scout position a throw bag relative to the target swimmer when casting across a moving current?
Why is it dangerous to tie a canoe's bow or stern painter line in a closed loop that can trail in the water?
Which label specifications verify that a personal flotation device is sized and approved for a youth paddler?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Standing a wooden paddle on its tip wicks moisture into the end grain and warps the blade; hang paddles by the grip or throat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Resting a wooden paddle vertically with its blade tip on a damp garage floor protects the shaft from warping.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Dragging a weighted canoe grinds down the keel and stem rapidly; always float the hull fully before loading or stepping inside.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Dragging a loaded aluminum or plastic canoe ten feet up a gravel boat ramp causes only cosmetic scratches.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Trapped moisture breeds mildew that weakens nylon webbing and rope fibers; unpack and air-dry rescue lines in the shade.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaving a wet throw bag packed tightly inside a sealed dry sack keeps the rescue line clean between trips.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tip-only support lets gravity sag the center hull over time; place padded racks upside down roughly one-third in from each end.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Supporting a stored canoe only at the extreme bow and stern tips keeps the middle of the hull straight.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a polyethylene or composite canoe hull stored right-side up outdoors where rainwater collects inside?
Why is it dangerous to dry wet life jackets over a campfire or hang them in direct summer sunlight for weeks?
Where should rack crossbars support an inverted canoe hull during winter storage to prevent gunwale sagging?
Which maintenance step prevents a wooden paddle tip from splitting and soaking up water after hitting gravel?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Stepping on a gunwale flips the hull immediately; crouch low, hold both gunwales, and place your foot dead center on the keel.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stepping onto the outer edge of the gunwale when boarding from a low dock helps push the canoe away from pilings.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Only one paddler moves at a time while staying low along the centerline as the partner braces the hull with knees spread wide.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Both tandem paddlers should stand up at the same time to switch bow and stern seats quickly on open water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A bow-heavy canoe catches water at the stem and lets wind spin the light stern; trim the hull level or slightly stern-heavy.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Trimming a canoe with the bow sitting two inches deeper than the stern makes the boat easier to steer in wind.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ramming the shore damages the stem and throws paddlers forward; back-paddle to stop before grounding and step out in ankle-deep water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Beaching a canoe at full paddling speed onto a sandy or rocky shore is the safest way for the bow paddler to step out dry.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout keep their hands and center of gravity while moving from a seat to a kneeling position afloat?
What happens to windage and steering control when a tandem canoe is trimmed bow-heavy by forty pounds?
Which paddler stabilizes the hull from the dock while their partner steps onto the centerline to board?
Under what water or wind condition should tandem paddlers drop from the seats to a three-point kneeling stance?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Shorelines look much closer than they are across open water, and a swamped canoe has built-in flotation to support both paddlers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Abandoning a swamped canoe in deep water to swim for a distant shoreline is safer than staying with the flooded hull.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Climbing over the narrow bow tips the boat; kick your legs to the surface at midfield and dolphin-kick flat across the gunwales.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pulling yourself straight up by both arms over the bow tip is the most stable way to reenter a canoe in deep water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A flooded canoe weighs hundreds of pounds; tip one end up onto the rescue boat's gunwale first to break suction and drain water.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Lifting a water-filled canoe straight up out of the lake is the fastest way to empty it during a deep-water rescue.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Clinging to the same gunwale rolls the hull toward the swimmers; position one paddler on each side to balance the swamped boat.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Both swimmers should hold onto the same side of a capsized canoe so they can talk while waiting for a rescue boat.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to reach under an overturned canoe before breaking the air seal at one end during a rescue?
Where should the assisting paddler lean while a swimmer kicks horizontally over the center gunwale to reenter?
What happens to a swamped canoe's buoyancy when two paddlers sit inside it and paddle toward shallow water?
Which step in a canoe-over-canoe rescue drains the water before the swamped hull is rolled upright on the gunwale?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tandem partners stay on opposite sides and maintain a straight course by paddling in unison while the stern applies a J-stroke.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Both tandem paddlers must switch paddle sides every few strokes to keep the canoe moving in a straight line.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The bow paddler sets the stroke cadence and rhythm, while the stern paddler matches that timing and controls directional alignment.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The bow paddler sets the steering direction from the front while the stern paddler watches and matches the new course.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Drawing on opposite sides spins the hull in a pivot; moving sideways requires one paddler to draw while the partner performs a pry.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Moving a tandem canoe sideways requires both partners to perform draw strokes simultaneously from opposite sides of the hull.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Kneeling on the hull bottom with knees braced wide against the sides lowers the center of gravity and maximizes roll stability.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sitting high on the seats with feet planted flat on the ribs gives tandem paddlers maximum stability during sharp turns.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the hull track when the stern paddler fails to match the bow paddler's stroke cadence?
Which blade angle adjustment lets the stern paddler correct yaw with a J-stroke instead of switching sides?
Under what waterline condition is a tandem canoe considered bow-heavy after partners swap positions on the water?
Why is it dangerous to lean your shoulders past the gunwale line while reaching out for a wide tandem draw stroke?
